newsitem.title: USA: Greenspan simply queried stock market level - Rubin.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan simply queried stock market level - Rubin.

text.p: Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan was merely raising a question last week about the level of the stock market, not voicing an opinion about whether prices are too high, Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said on Sunday.
"He was simply raising a question about levels of the market relative to fundamentals," Rubin told NBC television's "Meet the Press" program.

Greenspan sent world financial markets tumbling last Friday after he said the central bank needed to be wary when "irrational exuberance" infects stock and other asset markets because that could end up doing damage to the economy.

In a lecture on Thursday to the American Enterprise Institute, Greenspan stopped short of commenting on the recent steep run-up in Wall Street prices. But he made clear that the Fed would take the markets into account in setting policy.
"I interpret the chairman as simply raising a question. not suggesting an answer," Rubin said.
"Over time, markets do follow fundamentals and we've had very good fundamentals in this country for four years now," he added. "And we've had good markets as a consequence.
"The question is how are the markets at any given time relative to the fundamentals that exist," Rubin said.
Rubin made clear that Greenspan spoke on his own, and not on behalf of the Clinton administration. "He certainly spoke on his own advice," Rubin said.
The Treasury chief, who meets with Greenspan every week, indicated that he has was not surprised at the Fed chairman's remarks. "I had a sense he might at some point raise a question," Rubin said.
Despite repeated questioning, Rubin declined to say whether he thought stock prices were too high.

"What people really ought to be looking at is not these kind of day-to-day fluctuations (in the markets) but what they think economic conditions are going to be like over time, and are we going to do in this country the things we need to do ... to have the kind of economy and therefore the kind of markets we want to have," Rubin said.
Those measures include balancing the federal budget, which Rubin made clear was a top Clinton administration priority.
To help bring that about, Rubin left open the possibility of adjusting the Consumer Price Index (CPI), which is used to calculate cost-of-living increases for government benefits.

A congressionally-appointed commission last week concluded that the CPI overstates inflation by 1.1 percentage points per year, effectively costing the government billions of dollars per year in extra pension and other payments.
Rubin agreed that the CPI was an imperfect measure of inflation. "The question is, based on scientific and technical analysis, can we arrive at a better version of the CPI?"

"I don't think that we should rule out a change in the CPI if, based on a technical analysis, there is a broad-based agreement that the CPI can be changed in a such a way as to better, more accurately reflect inflation," Rubin added.
Rubin sounded cautious about proposals to privatize Social Security and allow the Social Security trust fund to invest in equities, not just Treasury bonds, in order to earn higher returns.
"Investing in equities, while an interesting idea, also has some concerns about it," he said. "And those concerns would have to be fully fleshed out, including the volatility of equities."
Rubin also signalled that he would be staying on as Treasury chief in President Clinton's second term, saying, "I think you'll likely see a relatively familiar face at Treasury."
